papers.title: System-Theoretic Analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models for Tumor Invasion
papers.abstract: The Cellular Potts Model has emerged as a standard framework for modeling multicellular systems and metastatic progression. Yet, computational extensions incorporating cell movement within spatial gradients of Extracellular Matrix (ECM), an important element of the tissue microenvironment, lack theoretical foundations. This work provides a system-theoretic formulation and analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models (ECPMs) that explicitly couple tumor dynamics with ECM degradation. We reformulate the ECPM as an interconnected dynamical system: a stochastic process describing a network of locally interacting tumor cells coupled to a jump-linear system describing ECM evolution. By exploiting the sparse energy structure of the model, we characterize asymptotic ECM behavior, transition probabilities with uniform bounds, and global system convergence. In one-dimensional settings, we derive closed-form expressions for invasion time probabilities, revealing how mean invasion time depends on local ECM gradients, number of cells and their tendency to maintain a target volume. Numerical simulations validate theoretical predictions, establishing a principled foundation for analyzing haptotaxis-driven invasion in Potts-based models.

papers.title: Morpheus.AI: agents autonomously generate, execute and refine virtual tissue models
papers.abstract: Virtual tissue models link observations to mechanistic hypotheses, but building them demands expertise in biology, mathematics and programming. Here, large language model (LLM) agents paired with the simulator Morpheus (Morpheus.AI) autonomously built such models from fifteen benchmark studies, five without a published model. With a frontier LLM, agents that ran their simulations met 83-86% of study-specific criteria in under two hours and for under US\$4 per model. Such agents could make in silico modeling routine.

papers.title: Spontaneous polarization for protrusion-driven cell crawling
papers.abstract: We propose a minimal one-dimensional continuum model for the spontaneous initiation of protrusion-driven cell crawling on a rigid substrate. The cell cytoskeleton is represented as a viscous actin meshwork that turns over in the bulk and polymerizes at two moving cell edges. Symmetry breaking arises from the feedback between cell motion, an external chemical regulator of actin nucleation, and actin polymerization at the cell fronts. When the cell moves, the regulator becomes polarized around the moving boundaries, thereby imposing different actin nucleation densities at the two edges. This generates unequal protrusive rates, which in turn reinforce motion and sustain the chemical polarization. Above a critical protrusive activity, the static symmetric state loses stability and the system undergoes a bifurcation toward a motile polarized state. Depending on how the external cue controls actin nucleation, the transition can be either supercritical or subcritical, leading in the latter case to coexistence between static and motile states. Using parameter values appropriate for keratocyte cells, the model predicts crawling speeds of the correct order of magnitude and actin-density profiles that are qualitatively similar to experimental observations, including asymmetric edge-localized density peaks. These results identify a generic mechanism by which external biochemical regulation of actin nucleation can trigger spontaneous motility along a one-dimensional track without requiring molecular motors, specific adhesion dynamics, deformable substrates, or pre-existing polarity.
